content: Orange County, Florida, receives an estimated 51 million visitors annually, with major attractions including Walt Disney World, Universal Orlando, and SeaWorld. The county seat is Orlando, Florida. The Florida Department of Health is responsible for a wide range of public health activities, including epidemiology, investigation of foodborne, zoonotic, and waterborne diseases, emergency preparedness and bioterrorism, communicable disease control, health promotion and education, school health, women’s health, public health dentistry and oral health, WIC and nutrition programs, vaccine-preventable diseases, addressing health disparities, provision of vital records, and environmental health protection. The department also maintains a hospital-based vital records office at Winter Park Memorial Hospital, part of Florida Hospital. Staff publications have included CDC Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report (MMWR) investigations into foodborne, waterborne, zoonotic, and other infectious diseases. Additionally, storyboards with graphics have been published by the Public Health Foundation in Washington, D.C., demonstrating how quality improvement efforts have enhanced public health outcomes related to sexually transmitted diseases (STDs) and HIV. The WIC and nutrition program staff collaborated with the Department of Health to publish a children’s book titled The Whole Grain Choo-Choo Train, which educates young children about proper eating habits and nutrition. In 2007, the deaths of three children in or near Orange County due to a rare and fatal infection, Primary Amoebic Meningoencephalitis (PAM), prompted a public health investigation in collaboration with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). PAM is a waterborne infection caused by the amoebic organism Naegleria fowleri, which enters the brain through the nose and is almost always fatal. This infection is associated with swimming and water sports in freshwater bodies and inadequately chlorinated swimming pools. The risk of Naegleria fowleri infections may increase with global climate change, as the organism thrives in warm water. Orange County, Florida, has recorded 12 cases of PAM over 45 years, out of 25 cases documented in the state of Florida. Globally, approximately 200 cases of PAM have been reported since 1990. The infection has been observed worldwide, including in colder climates such as the United Kingdom and Belgium. In 2007, additional PAM cases were reported in Texas and Arizona. The Orange County Health Department, the Florida Department of Health, and the CDC have also investigated other waterborne diseases, including giardiasis, cyclosporiasis, and cryptosporidiosis. Techniques for identifying cyclosporiasis were first developed in central Florida. These health authorities strongly recommend that swimmers and water sports enthusiasts wear nose plugs when ambient temperatures exceed 80 degrees Fahrenheit, particularly when engaging in freshwater activities.
